s: Late pre-Islamic warrior graves at the foot of Jabal Kawr · swords, arrowheads and bronze bowls
se: Near the village of Amlah, stone-lined graves held iron swords, daggers, 41 arrowheads in one grave, and bronze bowls with figures
sa: قرب قرية عملة، ضمّت قبور مبطّنة بالحجارة سيوفًا وخناجر من الحديد، و41 رأس سهم في قبر واحد، وأوعية برونزية مزيّنة بالرسوم
desc: A late pre-Islamic cemetery about 1 km east of the centre of Amlah and 2 km west of the foot of Jabal Kawr, published at N23°07′ E56°54′. Bank and Yule excavated 25 graves: 18 at al-Fueda, 5 at Qurain ar-Rusa and 2 in Wadi al-Mais. The graves are subterranean dry-stone chambers averaging 1.79 m long and 0.65 m wide, with floors about 1 m below the surface. Finds include 14 complete or lightly damaged pots, soft-stone vessels, four bronze bowls and iron weapons; one young man’s grave held three swords, a dagger and 41 arrowheads. The graves are assigned to phases PIR.A and PIR.B (late 3rd to 1st century BC).
sig: Its Samad-style graves with northern PIR-type goods suggest the late pre-Islamic culture of the north reached further south than once thought.
refs: Bank, C. & Yule, P. (2001). Al-Fueda near Amla, Sultanate of Oman. Proceedings of the Seminar for Arabian Studies 31, 15–22. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41223667
conf: Coordinates are the published point N23°07′ E56°54′ (Bank & Yule 2001), minute precision, ≈1–2 km. Timeline converted from the PIR.A–PIR.B centuries. Wikipedia gives 26 graves; the paper’s count of 25 is used. Arabic names الفويدة and عملة are careful transliterations to be checked.

s: Triassic limestone massif of the Oman Exotics · a volcanic eruption caught inside a carbonate platform
te: A reef that met a volcano
se: High above Ibri’s eastern oases, Jabal Kawr is a slab of Triassic sea limestone that once grew in a deep ocean basin, with ash from an ancient eruption inside it
sa: يرتفع جبل الكور فوق واحات عبري الشرقية، وهو كتلة من حجر جيري بحري تعود إلى العصر الترياسي، نمت يومًا في حوض محيطي عميق، وتحتضن رمادًا من ثوران بركاني قديم
desc: Jabal Kawr is a cliff-forming mountain on the eastern border of Ad Dhahirah; GeoNames gives its peak at 2,730 m and the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism about 2,700 m. Its carbonates belong to the Triassic Kawr (Kwar) Group of the Oman Exotics, which also builds Jabal Misht, Misfah and Ghul. Basile and Chauvet describe a phreatomagmatic eruption during the growth of this carbonate platform, which developed within the Hawasina basin; in their section the upper carbonate unit is about 150 m thick. The volcanic unit of the Misfah Formation has been dated Ladinian–Carnian from foraminifera, with a revised Norian to Rhaetian age proposed for its members. The mountain’s valleys feed the oases of Al-Abla and Al-Ain to the north and Nadan and Muwal to the west.
sig: One of the large Triassic exotic limestone blocks of the Oman Mountains, recording volcanism in the Neo-Tethys margin basin.
refs: Basile, C. & Chauvet, F. (2006). Phreatomagmatic eruption during the buildup of a Triassic carbonate platform (Oman Exotics): eruptive style, associated deformations, and implications on CO2 release by volcanism. HAL preprint hal-00116078. https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-00116078
GeoNames. Highest mountains in Oman (Jabal Kawr peak). https://www.geonames.org/OM/highest-mountains-in-oman.html
Ministry of Heritage and Tourism (Experience Oman). Ad Dhahirah guide. https://experienceoman.om/media/gi5b5zwi/ad-dhahira-en.pdf
conf: Coordinates are the GeoNames peak point (23.139, 57.014), ≈100 m. GeoNames lists the peak under Ad Dakhiliyah; the Ministry guide describes the mountain as on the eastern border of Al Dhahirah, so the region assignment should be checked. Timeline uses standard Ladinian start (≈242 Ma) and Rhaetian end (≈201 Ma) boundaries, not dates from the source. About 14 km from the existing Jebel Misht point. Arabic name جبل الكور follows common usage.

s: Warm spring flowing from a wadi near Nakhal Fort · feeds the aflaj of the oasis
se: Warm water bubbles out of the wadi near Nakhal Fort all year and runs through palm groves, where small fish nibble visitors’ feet
sa: يتدفق ماء دافئ من الوادي قرب حصن نخل طوال العام، ويجري بين بساتين النخيل حيث تداعب أسماك صغيرة أقدام الزوار
desc: A spring a few kilometres from Nakhal Fort, off the road between Barka and Rustaq in the Western Hajar mountains. Its water is warm rather than hot, despite a name linked to the Arabic word for boiling. The spring forms a stream in the wadi, and the Ministry of Regional Municipalities and Water Resources says hot water flows from the wadi continuously and is channelled into aflaj to irrigate nearby farms. A small rectangular concrete pool holds about 15 people, and a development project was reported as nearly 40% complete in 2023. In northern Oman, hot springs are associated with faults at the contact between Tertiary sediments and the Semail Ophiolite.
sig: A permanent spring that shows how groundwater rising along mountain-front faults sustains Oman’s oases and aflaj.
refs: Oman Observer (2017). A quick dip at Ain Al Thowarah. https://www.omanobserver.om/ampArticle/77900
Oman Observer (2020). Wilayat of Nakhl home to hot springs. https://www.omanobserver.om/article/6805/Oman/wilayat-of-nakhl-home-to-hot-springs
Oman Observer (2023). Work on Ain Al Thowarah hot springs 40% complete. https://www.omanobserver.om/article/1140911/oman/governorates/work-on-ain-althowarah-hot-springs-40-complete

Schütz, F., Winterleitner, G. & Huenges, E. (2018). Geothermal exploration in a sedimentary basin: new continuous temperature data and physical rock properties from northern Oman. Geothermal Energy 6, 5. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40517-018-0091-6
conf: Coordinates from Wikipedia (23°22′31″N 57°49′42″E), ≈50 m; pre-approved. No measured water temperature was found in the sources. The fault link is a general statement for northern Oman hot springs (Schütz et al. 2018), not a study of this spring. Timeline is a broad Quaternary estimate; the spring is not dated. About 2.2 km from the existing Nakhal Fort point, but a separate natural feature. Also 1.6 km from the existing Semail Ophiolite pin, which marks the whole ophiolite rather than this spring.

s: Mountain village of mud-and-stone houses and terraced fields below Jebel Shams
se: High in the Hajar Mountains, Bilad Sayt’s clustered houses sit above green terraces, reached only by four-wheel drive
sa: في أعالي جبال الحجر، تتجمع بيوت بلاد سيت فوق مدرّجات خضراء، ولا يُوصل إليها إلا بسيارات الدفع الرباعي
desc: A mountain village on the north-east slope of the Al Hajar Mountains near Jebel Shams, reached through Wadi Bani Awf and Wadi Al Sahtan from the north-east or from Al Hamra in the south-west. It is accessible only by four-wheel-drive vehicles. Its clustered mud-and-stone houses and terraced fields make it a noted heritage landscape, and the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism lists it among the most picturesque villages of South Al Batinah. Census figures give 2,404 people in 2003, 2,484 in 2010 and 3,567 in 2020.
sig: A living example of traditional Omani mountain agriculture, with terraces and stone houses adapted to steep slopes.
refs: Ministry of Heritage and Tourism (Experience Oman). Balad Sayt Village. https://experienceoman.om/destinations/al-batinah-south/balad-sayt-village
conf: Coordinates from Wikipedia (23°11′24.9″N 57°23′16.5″E), village point ≈200 m; pre-approved. Region follows the Ministry’s Experience Oman (Al Batinah South); Wikipedia places it in Wilayat Bahla, Ad Dakhiliyah, so this should be checked. No founding date is published: t0 (about 500 years) is a broad estimate for the traditional village. Arabic name from Wikipedia; the Ministry romanises it Balad Sayt.
